newsitem.title: SOUTH AFRICA: S.AFRICAN BUILDERS SEEN VITAL TO JOB CREATION.
newsitem.headline: S.AFRICAN BUILDERS SEEN VITAL TO JOB CREATION.

text.p: The department of public works was examining ways in which the construction sector could play a bigger role in job creation, deputy director general Lulu Gwagwa said on Thursday.

Briefing the parliamentary finance committee, Gwagwa said that it was recognised that government had found it difficult to "offload" funds set aside for infrastructural projects and several initiatives had been launched to increase its ability to plan and implement projects.
But it would be a mistake to focus only on this problem because the ability of the industry to absorb these funds also had to be examined.
"It is an issue that we are debating with the industry at the moment," she said.

"But you could offload money and industry could absorb it and you could land up with infrastructure and no jobs. It does not necessary follow that if you invest in infrastructure, that you will necessarily have job creation within that framework.
"What is important is whether industry is able to adopt job creation strategies in the implementation of that infrastructure and for us that is the critical issue.

"There are a whole lot of issues that we are raising with the industry and there is a green paper that is going to be coming out in the next month addressing the transformation of the construction industry," she said.

South African Federation of Civil Engineering Contractors economist Hank Langenhoven told the committee earlier that the construction industry was concerned about bottlenecks in the allocation of funds set aside for infrastructural problems.
Several committee members said that they could not understand why the private sector, which had generally shown improved profitability since 1994, had not been able to increase jobs at the same time.
Chamber of Mines public policy consultant Johann Liebenberg said that business was not in business to create jobs.

"We use a mix of labour capital, natural resources and entrepreneurship to do something else and the decision as to how one makes up that mix depends on all the factors and circumstances existing at that moment in time," he said.

The sharp increase in private sector fixed investment over the last few years would not immediately translate into more jobs, especially when the immediate priority was to update machinery and equipment neglected during the sanctions period.
Job creation would also be stimulated in the longer term if local and foreign investors felt confident about government policies.

Business South Africa representative and economist Rudolph Gouws said that the recent budget had re-established investor confidence although there were still concerns about high taxation and the feasibility of tight government spending targets.
